source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming (Table 1, Appendix E.3, G)
finding: Table 1 re-read with raw text extraction (gap 7). Cells: JBB classifier, PAIR (Mixtral) -/4, PAIR with Rainbow Teaming's mutator LLM 1/1, Rainbow Teaming 8/7. Llama Guard: PAIR (Mixtral) not reported, PAIR with RT mutator 14/11, Rainbow Teaming 66/41. Self-BLEU (lower is more diverse): PAIR 0.74, Rainbow Teaming 0.51. So the earlier '1 across 1' figure was the JBB-classifier cell, not the Llama Guard cell. Corrects c12/b20.
numbers: (n jailbreaks / k behaviours of 100). JBB classifier: PAIR-Mixtral -/4, PAIR-RT-mutator 1/1, RT 8/7. Llama Guard: PAIR-RT-mutator 14/11, RT 66/41. Self-BLEU 0.74 vs 0.51. Best of 4 regenerated responses per prompt.
quote: Compared to both PAIR variants, Rainbow Teaming discovers more jailbreaks across more behaviours
limits: PAIR got 2,000 prompts (N=20 parallel streams) but Rainbow Teaming only 1,000 prompts, so the budget was not in QD's favour. No PAIR restarts or same-budget archive-free diversification were run. One mutator LLM, one target, single run per cell (no error bars in Table 1). The '-/4' cell is a 4-behaviour count with the jailbreak total missing.
agent_relevance: The QD gain over a one-solution-per-stream optimiser is large even when the baseline gets twice the prompts. But the domain has a cheap classifier and many separate targets (100 behaviours); our reasoning tasks have one target per item.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming (Appendix G inference cost; Appendix E.3 judge agreement)
finding: Overhead share (gap 10). One loop costs 2 mutator calls, 1 target call and 4 judge calls. The judge is 4 of 7 calls (57%). 2,000 iterations = 14,000 batched calls per run, about two days on 128 to 256 A100 GPUs. Judge agreement: human-human 83%, human-GPT-4 81%, human-Llama Guard 78%, GPT-4 vs Llama Guard 79% (100 pairs, 4 annotators).
numbers: 7 calls per iteration; judge share 4/7; 14,000 batched calls per 2,000-iteration run; batch 16 (64 for JBB); agreement 78-83%.
limits: Counts calls, not tokens. Descriptor labelling is folded into the mutator calls, so its own share is not separable. The authors call the compute 'substantial'.
agent_relevance: Judging, not generation, dominates the call budget of a QD loop. At equal tokens a loop spends more than half on scoring; our agent must count judge tokens inside the budget.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Evolving Deeper LLM Thinking (Mind Evolution) Tables 2, 4, 5
finding: Ablations (gap 2). On TravelPlanner validation (Gemini 1.5 Flash) success rates across the component-ablation columns were 46.1%, 71.1%, 76.1%, 91.1%, 95.6% as components (critic, strategy/question prompts, textual feedback, LLM-based island reset) were switched on; full system 95.6%. The authors say the critic step and evaluator textual feedback matter most. Island model on 10-city Trip Planning at 800 candidates: 87.5% with 4 islands vs 77.4% with 1 island. Best-of-N 55.6% and Sequential-Revision+ 82.8% on TravelPlanner val; the authors say Best-of-N fails because it cannot learn implicit constraints from evaluator feedback.
numbers: TravelPlanner val: BoN 100/180=55.6%, SeqRev+ 149/180=82.8%, Mind Evolution 172/180=95.6%. Islands: 87.5% vs 77.4% (about 10 points, 800 candidates). Convs/gens split: 82.5% (10,5), 87.5% (5,10), 85.0% (4,13).
limits: The ablation table layout is garbled in extraction, so which column maps to which rate is uncertain; only the ordering and end points (46.1% to 95.6%) are safe. No recombination-only ablation exists. Every task uses a programmatic evaluator giving textual feedback, so critic gain is conflated with verifier quality. Single runs, no error bars stated.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain over Best-of-N comes from using evaluator feedback and the critic (a refinement loop); islands add about 10 points on top. The archive/island part is a minority share. A model-only-verifier version was not tested.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Evolving Deeper LLM Thinking, StegPoet and cost tables
finding: On the StegPoet task Best-of-N reached 1/101 (1.0%) and 1-Pass 0/101, so plain sampling fails when the target is a rare conjunction of constraints. In the readable cells of the cost table Mind Evolution used about as many input tokens as Best-of-N on TravelPlanner (3.0M vs 3.1M); the rest of the cost table is garbled.
numbers: StegPoet: 1-Pass 0/101, Best-of-N 1/101. TravelPlanner input tokens: BoN 3.10M, ME about 3.02-3.05M.
limits: Cost table partly garbled; the token-matching reading rests on two readable cells. Evaluator is programmatic.
agent_relevance: The matched-cost comparison with best-of-N is the authors' own design, so the headline is roughly cost-matched, but only with a checker.

source: Vijayakumar et al. (2025) NoveltyBench, Section 4.3 alternate prompting
finding: Gap 6. Four sampling methods on 100 curated prompts, 8 generations each, Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro: resampling, paraphrasing, system prompt, and in-context regeneration (keep all earlier answers in context and ask for a different one). Only in-context regeneration roughly matched the diversity of 8 human authors; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro even exceeded human cumulative utility. Paraphrase and system prompt were only marginal.
numbers: 100 prompts, 8 generations, 3 models; effect shown only in a figure (distinct generations out of 8), exact counts not in text.
quote: Paraphrasing and system prompting are only marginally effective
limits: Open-ended prompts with many valid answers, no correctness measure for one-right-answer tasks. No comparison with an archive loop or a descriptor-guided loop, and no token cost (context grows with each turn). Distinct count is judged by a classifier, not by solve rate.
agent_relevance: Showing prior answers is a strong cheap baseline for distinct outputs. It has not been compared with an archive loop on solve rate, so gap 6 stays open, but it sets the cost floor any archive must beat.

source: Donaghy and Rastogi (2026) DEI: Diversity in Evolutionary Inference for Quality-Diversity Search
finding: Gaps 8 and 1. In Core War (Redcode warriors) at equal total LLM-call budget (250 calls per round), a 4-model heterogeneous ensemble gave a merged archive with QD-Score 45.90 and 80.6% coverage vs 20.46 and 63.0% for one solo node; a same-model 4-node ensemble gave 29.85 and 59.0%. Some gain came from parallel nodes sharing elites and most from model heterogeneity. This contrasts with NoveltyBench's finding that models agree with each other.
numbers: Solo 63.0% / 20.46; homogeneous merged 59.0% / 29.85; diverse merged 80.6% / 45.90. Four nodes x 62 iterations vs solo 250 calls.
limits: Company preprint, one domain (Core War), run count not stated in the text I read, no best-of-N or no-archive control, quality measured as fitness against opponents. Not a reasoning task.
agent_relevance: Mixing model families can enlarge archive coverage at equal calls in a code domain. We use one agent, so only the idea of different priors (personas or methods) transfers, untested.

source: Land (2026) Modality-Driven Search with Holistic Trace Judging for ARC-AGI-2
finding: Gap 1. Closest ARC system to a diversity-first loop: independent candidates across text, image and code channels (up to 29 per task), then one judge reads all traces together. Score 72.9% at $38.99 per task on the semi-private set, 76.1% at $19.69 on the public set. Judge selection beat plain majority vote by net +7 solved tasks on the public set, all minority recoveries (in one task 12 candidates gave one wrong answer, 8 another, 1 the right one). Synthesis added +1. The author lists as NOT done: independent vs sequential at equal compute, candidate-budget scaling, modality ablation, 1 vs 3 judges; no confidence intervals.
numbers: 72.9% at $38.99/task (semi-private); 76.1% at $19.69/task (public); judge vs majority vote +7 tasks; synthesis +1; GPT-5.2 Pro 54.2%, Gemini 3 Pro 54.0%.
quote: reliably recovers correct minority hypotheses on tasks where the modal answer is wrong
limits: Solo author, single run, ablations skipped for cost; descriptor is the reasoning modality (a hand-chosen coarse label), no archive loop, no matched best-of-N or duplicate-filter control. Gains come from judging as much as from diversity.
agent_relevance: Supports 'diversify the method channel, then pick with a judge that reads the traces' over majority vote. It does not show that a QD archive beats best-of-N at equal tokens, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve, Section 4 Ablations
finding: Gap 8. Ablations on two tasks (tensor decomposition, kissing numbers), curves versus compute fraction, averaged over 3 seeds. Conditions: full method, no evolution (feed the same initial program repeatedly), no context in prompt, no meta-prompt evolution, no full-file evolution, small base LLM only. Text says each component helps. The 'no evolution' control removes the whole database, so it cannot split MAP-Elites from islands; no archive-vs-no-archive control with the same prompt context exists.
numbers: 3 independent seeds per setting; numbers only in Figure 8 (not readable in text).
limits: Figure-only results, only 3 seeds, authors' own system, strong closed models. 'No evolution' conflates database, parent sampling and inspirations. The database is described as inspired by MAP-Elites and island models.
agent_relevance: Evolving from history beats repeated fresh calls on these tasks, but the unique value of descriptor-keyed cells is still not isolated.

source: Lange, Imajuku, Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve, Section 5 ablations
finding: Gap 8, 10. Open-source framework with ablations on circle packing. Parent selection: best-of-N (always the seed program) worst, hill climbing fast then plateaus, weighted sampling by fitness and offspring count wins. Bandit LLM-ensemble beats single model and fixed ensemble. Embedding rejection (cosine over 0.95) beats none; the extra LLM novelty judge adds only a marginal gain, so the authors say embedding is enough without extra computational overhead. Circle-packing record with 150 samples.
numbers: 150 evaluations for the circle-packing result; threshold 0.95; seed count for ablations not stated in the text I read.
limits: Authors' own system, curves only, seeds unstated, no archive-free control with matched context. No overhead share in tokens or seconds is reported. The authors list the lack of automatic exploration-exploitation control as a limitation.
agent_relevance: Embedding dedup is a cheap, measured part of the loop; the judge-based novelty check is not worth its extra calls. Hill climbing plateaus, so exploit-only is a known failure.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Gap 5, verifier versus no verifier. MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage (any sample correct) 82.9% at 100 samples, 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward-model selection rose only from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. Where an automatic verifier exists (code tests, Lean), coverage converts to success; where it does not, selection plateaus near 100 samples. SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% to 56% with repeated sampling and a test-based check. False-positive solutions that pass weak tests are noted.
numbers: MATH coverage 82.9% to 98.44% vs selection 40.50% to 41.41%; SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56%.
quote: common methods for picking from a sample collection (majority voting and reward models) plateau beyond several
limits: Measures repeated sampling, not QD; reward model was ArmoRM-8B, a weak judge. Shows the verifier gap but not a gap for a QD quality score specifically.
agent_relevance: Diversity only helps if selection can find the rare correct sample. With a model judge instead of a checker, extra distinct attempts mostly add cost. About 57 points separate coverage from selection on maths.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2023) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: Gap 5. With a synthetic gold reward model, optimising against a proxy reward model first raises then lowers the gold score, for both best-of-n and RL. Fitted forms: best-of-n gold R(d)=d(alpha - beta d), RL R(d)=d(alpha - beta log d), with d the square root of KL. Larger proxies and more proxy data overoptimise less; policy size matters little.
numbers: Functional forms fitted over proxy sizes and data sizes; coefficients vary smoothly (about log) with proxy parameter count.
limits: Learned preference reward model with synthetic gold labels, not LLM judges of diversity or code. Gives the shape of the gap, not a QDAIF number.
agent_relevance: More best-of-n against a judge past an optimum lowers true quality; cap judge-guided selection pressure and prefer a held-out or programmatic check.

source: Shihab and Afrin (2026) Quality-Diversity Stress Tests for Process Reward Models
finding: Gap 5. MAP-Elites used as an attacker finds correctness-flipping edits to reasoning traces that a learned PRM still scores high. Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B with mean pooling: 44 strict exploits, maximum gain 0.294, while minimum readout gives 1 exploit. How step scores are aggregated changes hackability a lot. A coverage fraction alone cannot bound the worst remaining cell.
numbers: 44 strict mean-readout exploits vs 1 under min readout; max gain 0.294; RLHFlow value-head model max gain 0.005; problem-level mean-readout exploit rate 0.232 [0.146, 0.329].
limits: Preprint, GSM8K-style traces, two PRMs, hand-designed descriptor.
agent_relevance: A model verifier is hackable by edits that look like checking; use a min-style or hard check rather than an average of step scores.

source: Conti et al. (2018) Improving Exploration in Evolution Strategies via a Population of Novelty-Seeking Agents (NS-ES, NSR-ES, NSRA-ES)
finding: Gap 4 and 9. Hybrid with an adaptive weight w between reward and novelty. NSRA-ES starts at w=1.0 (reward only), lowers w by 0.05 if the best reward does not rise for 50 generations, raises w when a new best is found. On 12 Atari games: NSRA-ES best on 5/12, beats ES on 8/12 and NSR-ES on 9/12. ES got stuck in a local optimum in 5 games (Seaquest, Q*Bert, Freeway, Beam Rider, Frostbite) where NSR-ES won; in the other games exploration cost reward. With w changed every 50 generations by 0.05, NSRA-ES stayed in the Seaquest trap; every 10 generations fixed it (NSR-ES median 2329.7 on Seaquest).
numbers: Atari median of 5 runs; humanoid 10 runs; Mann-Whitney U tests; stagnation window 50 generations, step 0.05.
quote: NSRA-ES optimizes solely for reward until a performance plateau is reached.
limits: Plateau signal and step sizes were set without hyperparameter search and were too slow in one game. RL parameter-space ES, not LLM. Behaviour characteristic (RAM states) hand-picked.
agent_relevance: A measured switch rule: exploit first, count stagnation, then add exploration pressure, and go back when progress resumes. Easy to copy as 'if the best score has not improved in k tries, force a different method'; k needs tuning.

source: Conti et al. (2018) NS-ES paper: non-deceptive cases
finding: Negative result on a real control task (gap 9). The standard humanoid walking problem 'does not appear to be a deceptive problem, at least for ES': pure novelty search (NS-ES) reached lower final reward than ES and the gap was larger at small compute. They say a behaviour space covering every part of the reward would be needed to close the gap, and would raise compute. In many Atari games novelty alone did not give higher reward.
numbers: ES > NS-ES and NSR-ES, p<0.05 each, after 600 generations; NSRA-ES vs ES p>0.05.
limits: One paper, one task family; shows the cost of novelty when the objective is fine.
agent_relevance: Pure novelty loses on tasks where plain optimisation works; most reasoning items with one right answer are like that, which argues for a reward-first hybrid.

source: Colas, Sigaud, Oudeyer (2018) GEP-PG: Decoupling Exploration and Exploitation in Deep RL
finding: Gap 4. Fixed two-stage switch: a goal-exploration process fills the replay buffer, then DDPG exploits. On the deceptive Continuous Mountain Car, GEP reached the goal in about 3,800 steps while DDPG with parameter or action noise reached it before 50,000 steps in only 42% or 22% of trials. On Half-Cheetah GEP-PG with parameter noise reached 5,740 (std 573) against DDPG 4,961 (1,288); GEP alone was worse (2,105). Stable for 100 to 600 exploration episodes; the buffer needs both good and diverse trajectories.
numbers: 20 seeds per condition. HC final metric: DDPG-param 4961 (1288), GEP-PG-param 5740 (573), GEP-param 2105 (881).
limits: Switch point fixed by hand, not a measured budget fraction; no policy transfer at the switch (performance drops). Continuous control only.
agent_relevance: Handing exploration output to an exploiter works and is robust to the switch point over a wide range, at a small share of budget. The best rule is still untested for token-limited agents.

source: Boldi, Ding, Spector (2023) Objectives Are All You Need: Solving Deceptive Problems Without Explicit Diversity Maintenance
finding: Gap 9, competing explanation. Lexicase selection over many sub-aggregated objectives beat MAP-Elites on deceptive Knight's Tour and deceptive maze, and matched or beat it on QD-Score and coverage without optimising for them. On a non-deceptive maze all methods reached the optimum, lexicase still had higher QD-Score, and QD wins on pure illumination domains. Means over 10 replicates.
numbers: 10 replicate runs per method; 16 and 64 objectives beat MAP-Elites on the deceptive maze.
limits: Workshop paper, hand-built domains, descriptor hand-crafted for MAP-Elites.
agent_relevance: Splitting the objective into many sub-checks (per example or per constraint) can give diversity for free; scoring a candidate on separate test cases may stand in for an archive.

source: Chenu, Perrin-Gilbert, Doncieux, Sigaud (2021) Selection-Expansion: Unifying Motion-Planning and Diversity Search
finding: Gap 3. Diversity search (novelty search, goal exploration) explores as well as motion-planning only if the map from parameters to outcome descriptor is smooth: similar policies yield similar outcomes. Without smoothness, performance depends strongly on the mapping and diversity in descriptor space no longer explores efficiently.
numbers: No single headline number extracted; shown on two environments with and without a smooth mapping.
limits: Robot control, hand-designed outcome spaces. Argument by two environments.
agent_relevance: A good LLM descriptor must change slowly under small edits to an attempt and track what matters for success. Method-class labels are coarse and may be stable, but this was not measured.
